problems.description: Concurrency model mixes asyncio (WebSocket loop) with a threading-based HTTP health server sharing one registry (complexity +9); workable because all registry access is lock-guarded, but the split adds coordination surface that could be avoided with a single asyncio HTTP server.
_HealthHandler reaches into self.server.owner via a type-ignore comment rather than a typed injection point, a fragile coupling between handler and server.
Module-level default instance `server = NotificationServer()` creates a process-wide singleton with non-obvious lifecycle; port fields are also silently mutated in start() to actual bound ports.
test_notification_server.py violates project conventions: classes not PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (convention score 0.82).

strengths: Coherent single-file architecture: async WebSocket loop, health HTTP endpoint, and lock-protected shared registry with graceful shutdown for both servers.
Zero new bugs, two fewer smells, and no duplication (SonarQube delta: bugs +0, smells -2, duplications 0.0%).
Full type hints on public signatures, snake_case functions, PascalCase classes, and informative docstrings; main module is convention-clean (violations confined to tests).
Defensive message handling: invalid JSON, non-dict payloads, and unsupported types are rejected safely.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured greenfield rewrite that delivers the requested async notification service with clean, lock-guarded concurrency and zero regressions, marred only by minor coupling and test-file convention slips.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +59 for a 66-line change: _handle_message now overloads the `channel` variable to mean three different things (subscription key, routing filter, outgoing-field) across subscribe/unsubscribe/direct/broadcast branches, making the dispatch hard to follow.
Duplications +10.3%: the unsubscribe branch duplicates the disconnect-cleanup logic (discard from channels, prune empty channel) instead of extracting a shared helper, so the two paths can drift.
No tests accompany the new subscribe/unsubscribe flow or the /channels and /channels/<name>/subscribers endpoints (+0 test functions); the newly added channel-filtered routing logic is untested.

Channel resolution falls back to payload.get("channel"), so a payload-supplied channel silently alters broadcast/direct routing semantics versus a top-level channel field, creating ambiguity about which value wins.

Discrepancy: AST reports +0 functions despite two new methods (channel_counts, channel_subscribers); the convention violations are attributed to test_notification_server.py which is not part of this diff, suggesting the 0.82 score reflects pre-existing code.

strengths: Extends the existing registry-plus-lock pattern consistently (client_channels/channels mirror the clients dict), and reuses the established message shape and timestamp() helper.
Subscription bookkeeping is pruned correctly on both unsubscribe and disconnect, removing empty channel entries so the registry never leaks stale state.
Health endpoint grows channel introspection with URL-decoding and a path validation guard (rejects embedded '/' after unquote) to prevent channel-path traversal.
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally solid feature addition that faithfully follows the server's existing registry/lock patterns but introduces notable complexity and duplication for its size, plus leaves the new subscription/routing paths untested.

problems.description: The diff compresses multi-line control flow into one-liners (e.g. `if not subscribers: self.channels.pop(channel, None)` and semicolon-chained `self.clients.clear(); self.client_channels.clear()`), a readability regression from the original style; consistent with SonarQube +28 cognitive complexity and +3 smells.
In `start()`, `except Exception: await self._close_redis()` swallows Redis connection failures silently — the server continues without the pub/sub backbone with no logging or telemetry signal.
`except ImportError: Redis = Any` weakens type safety; a runtime-gated import or Protocol-based seam would be cleaner than assigning a type alias to `Any`.

The cross-instance pub/sub test uses a busy-wait poll loop (20 × 10ms) on Redis client state instead of awaiting an event, which is flake-prone and couples the assertion to internal Redis key naming (`notifications:client:{id}`).

Mechanical convention score 0.82; both flagged violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE constant) are in test_notification_server.py. Note the score is computed on final worktree state, so these may partly predate this commit — app.py changes themselves are convention-clean.

strengths: Full Session 3 spec coverage: Redis pub/sub backbone, client connection state stored in Redis, SQLite persistence, `/messages?limit&offset` endpoint, and REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL env config.
Injectable `redis_client` enables fakeredis-based integration tests without a real broker, and graceful local-delivery fallback when Redis is unavailable.
`MessageStore` cleanly encapsulates SQLite persistence behind a thread lock with blocking I/O offloaded via `asyncio.to_thread`.
Origin-tagging on published envelopes prevents self-echo across instances; existing API and behavior preserved with all 6 tests passing, no new bugs, and 0% duplication.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped, spec-complete Redis+SQLite integration that respects the existing architecture and passes all tests, marred only by a compressed one-liner style and minor resilience/type-safety concerns.

problems.description: Concurrency regression: `registry_lock` still guards reads of `self.clients` in `client_count` (health thread), but all writers now live in the transport (`on_connect`/`on_disconnect`/`stop` mutate the shared dict without acquiring the lock). The lock no longer protects the dict it was designed for, so the health-server thread can observe an in-flux dict.

Robustness regression on the direct-send path: `WebSocketTransport.send_message` calls `connection.send` with no `ConnectionClosed` guard, and `_deliver`'s direct branch plus `_on_client_connect` invoke it unshielded. The pre-refactor code wrapped all sends in `gather(..., return_exceptions=True)`; only `broadcast` still does.

The new abstraction and its factory are untested in isolation: no unit tests for `BaseTransport`/`WebSocketTransport`, and the `_create_transport` env-selection branch (incl. the ValueError on unsupported transport) is uncovered — existing tests only exercise it indirectly.

Inconsistent optional-method contract: `BaseTransport.start` raises NotImplementedError while `BaseTransport.stop` is a bare no-op docstring stub, and neither is decorated `@abstractmethod` — divergent signals for the two lifecycle hooks.
`from abc import ABC, abstractmethod` was inserted after the `from http.server import ...` block, breaking stdlib import alphabetical ordering.

strengths: Clean `BaseTransport` ABC seam (on_connect/on_disconnect/send_message/broadcast + TRANSPORT env factory, WebSocketTransport default) that exactly implements the session-4 brief and decouples the server core from the websockets library
Constructor injection of `transport` follows the existing DI pattern (`redis_client`, `database_url`); public API preserved and all existing tests pass unmodified
Single source of truth for connections via `self.clients = self.transport.clients` aliasing, avoiding the dual-registry drift seen in other refactor variants
Measured improvements confirm the value: cognitive complexity -35, smells -2, +0 bugs, +0.0% duplication, +2 classes/+1 import only
Dynamic-port preservation (`transport.start` returns the bound port) keeps health/metrics behavior intact
commit_reviews.summary: A genuinely architectural refactor that cleanly extracts a pluggable transport layer with measured complexity/smell reductions and zero behavior change, marred only by minor latent concurrency-lock and unshielded direct-send regressions; the reported 0.82 convention score is repo-wide and stems from two violations in test_notification_server.py, a file this commit does not touch, so the commit's own diff is convention-clean.

problems.description: rate_limit == 0 disables all non-control messages (returns False in _allow_message), so setting RATE_LIMIT=0 denies service entirely instead of disabling the limit — the semantics contradict what a 0/negative value convention would imply. SonarQube reported +0 bugs, so this edge-case logic flaw is a discrepancy vs the mechanical measurement.
MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS=0 (or unset-default semantics) makes the cleanup cutoff equal 'now', deleting all stored history on the first cleanup cycle; a 0 TTL should arguably mean 'never delete'.
Cognitive complexity increased by +35 (SonarQube delta); the _handle_message dispatch and _allow_message dual-path (Redis/local) logic grew significantly, though smells decreased by -2.
Two convention violations in test_notification_server.py: test class not in PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (consistent with the 0.82 convention score).

strengths: Extracted shared _query() helper, removing duplicated row-mapping/connection-guard logic from list() and history()
New cross-cutting features (history, rate limiting, TTL cleanup) are added as isolated methods on MessageStore/NotificationServer, respecting the existing store/handler/transport layering
Rate limiting mirrors the established Redis-with-local-fallback pattern already used by the pub/sub transport
Cleanup task lifecycle follows the _subscriber_task pattern: created in start(), cancelled and awaited in stop()
Parameterized queries throughout; no SQL injection surface introduced
Tests added for the new rate-limit behavior
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit that cleanly adds history, rate limiting, and message TTL cleanup while refactoring duplication into a shared query helper — the only meaningful concerns being the counter-intuitive rate-limit/TTL zero-value semantics and the test-file naming violations (0.82 convention score).

compounding_issues: Session 1 fully discarded the seeded codebase (a Flask todo API) in favor of a greenfield async WebSocket rewrite, so the entire story rests on that single architectural decision rather than building on the seed's seams.

The threaded-HTTP + async-WebSocket hybrid with one shared registry_lock forced every later HTTP feature (/channels, /messages, /history) to route registry and SQLite access through the lock and asyncio.to_thread, constraining how S3 and S5 could be built.

Session 4's transport refactor aliased transport.clients to NotificationServer.clients but moved client mutations outside registry_lock (WebSocketTransport.on_connect/on_disconnect/broadcast mutate without the lock), weakening the thread-safety discipline S2/S3 had established; latent race, never triggered by tests.

Session 5's /history chronological pagination trusts client-supplied timestamps (message.get('timestamp') or timestamp()) and string-compares ISO values in SQL, so out-of-order or forged client timestamps can corrupt pagination order.

Rate limiter default (RATE_LIMIT=100) only guards non-subscribe messages and is a local-window fallback when Redis is absent, so behavior silently diverges between single-instance and Redis deployments.
key_decisions: S1: single-file async server using the websockets library with a stdlib ThreadingHTTPServer for /health and a threading.Lock-guarded shared client registry.
S2: bidirectional channel subscription model (client_channels + channels maps) with subscribe/unsubscribe message types and channel-scoped routing for broadcast and direct delivery.
S3: Redis pub/sub backbone for multi-instance distribution with instance-id echo suppression, plus a SQLite MessageStore (JSON payloads) and Redis client-state hashes.
S4: BaseTransport ABC / WebSocketTransport abstraction to decouple connection lifecycle from routing, selectable via TRANSPORT env var — the foundation that made S5 clean.

S5: Redis-backed fixed-window rate limiting with a local fallback, /history channel+since+limit pagination endpoint, and a background TTL cleanup loop, all env-configurable via RATE_LIMIT and MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. The story began with a clean, well-tested single-process MVP (4 tests) in S1, then layered on a channel subscription model in S2 without breaking existing behavior. S3 added real infrastructure — Redis pub/sub fan-out, SQLite persistence, and a paginated /messages endpoint — growing tests to 6. S4 was a stabilizing refactor that extracted a transport abstraction while keeping all behavior and tests intact, which directly enabled S5's cross-cutting features (rate limiting, chronological /history, TTL cleanup). Test coverage grew monotonically (4 → 6 → 8) and the full suite passed at the final commit, indicating the architecture absorbed each new capability rather than collapsing under it.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-staged story in which the agent evolved a simple notification MVP into a durable, multi-instance, rate-limited service through deliberate feature-integration-refactor-cross-cutting steps, keeping tests green and quality climbing throughout.
